prompt.en: A whole-cable ferrite reduces RF that flows the same way on both power leads, but a different noise current flowing out on one lead and back on the other remains. Why?

text.en: The ferrite has proved that every remaining noise source must be inside the receiver.

feedback.en: A remaining symptom does not locate its source. The two current paths respond differently.

text.en: All noise follows the same path, so the ferrite must have failed between tests.

feedback.en: The observations describe common-mode and differential-mode currents, not necessarily a failed part.

text.en: The first current was common mode; the second is differential mode and may need a different filter.

feedback.en: A whole-cable choke mainly impedes common-mode RF. It is not a universal cure for differential noise.

text.en: A ferrite should mainly block the intended DC current, so both tests used the wrong principle.

feedback.en: The intended out-and-back current is usually left mostly unchanged; unwanted common-mode current is the target.

explanation.en: Identify how the unwanted current travels before expecting the same cure to work on every noise path.

prompt.en: A narrower IF filter removes an adjacent tone from the audio, but a strong off-band source still desensitizes the receiver. What does that result show?

text.en: The IF filter helps later selectivity but cannot undo overload that already happened at the front end.

feedback.en: The two symptoms occur at different stages. The strong off-band energy must be reduced before the input stage overloads.

text.en: Any successful IF filtering proves that the front end is operating linearly.

feedback.en: Removing a later unwanted tone does not establish adequate headroom in the earlier input stage.

text.en: An input attenuator is a cost-free cure that leaves weak wanted levels unchanged.

feedback.en: Attenuation can help overload but also reduces the wanted weak signal. A suitable input filter is preferable when the frequencies can be separated.

text.en: More RF gain must restore sensitivity regardless of the strong off-band source.

feedback.en: Extra input gain can worsen overload. It does not remove the strong signal that uses up front-end headroom.

explanation.en: A partial improvement can identify one stage without curing a separate earlier-stage problem.

prompt.en: A filter rejects the unwanted frequency correctly, but it was designed for a different nominal impedance than the receiver line. Why can wanted-signal delivery still suffer?

text.en: Correct rejection frequency guarantees that all wanted power passes without reflection.

feedback.en: Frequency response alone does not guarantee a good system match.

text.en: An impedance mismatch can cause reflections and loss even when the rejected frequency is right.

feedback.en: Match the filter to the line and equipment as well as choosing the correct response.

text.en: The filter's centre frequency automatically changes the line's characteristic impedance.

feedback.en: The cable's geometry and dielectric set its Z0. Inserting a mismatched network does not redefine the whole line.

text.en: Adding coax until the station-end reading looks better guarantees that the filter is now matched internally.

feedback.en: Line length can transform a measured impedance under mismatch. It does not make a filter designed for a different impedance equivalent to a correctly matched filter.

explanation.en: Frequency selection, impedance, and placement are separate filter requirements.
